newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand says baht adjustment won't help c/a woes.
newsitem.headline: Thailand says baht adjustment won't help c/a woes.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Wednesday that adjustment of the baht and exchange rate system would not solve the current account deficit problem.

Speaking at a closed seminar organised by Morgan Stanley, Amnuay said the new government, which took office last week, preferred to boost performance of the foreign exchange earning sector to narrow the gap.

The baht is fixed daily by the central bank against a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar. The central bank allows the baht to fluctuate within a narrow four-satang band when it buys or sells dollars from banks.

"I must stress that I do not believe that the adjustment in the value of the baht and the exchange rate system will be the ultimate solution to this particular problem," he said in a copy of his speech obtained by Reuters.
"Rather, to solve the current account deficit problem, measures must be put in place to help our exporters to reduce their production cost and add value to their product," he said.

Phenomenal sluggishness in exports this year has put pressure on the ballooning current account deficit which is expected to widen to 8.2-8.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) for 1996. In 1995, it was 8.1 percent of GDP.

Sluggish exports, which recorded growth of only 0.9 percent during the first nine months of 1996 compared to 20 percent during the same period last year, had sparked speculation that the baht could be devalued to boost competitiveness.

Despite the stagnant exports, Amnuay said he expected Thailand's GDP growth to be around seven percent this year due to the domestic market strengthening. Private analysts have put growth this year at just over six percent.

On the depressed Thai property market, he said: "A way out must be found for the problem of the property sector. In this respect we must look for a way that would stimulate and raise demand from both domestic and foreign investors."

Amnuay said he would seek to restore investor confidence in Thailand. "Thailand is presently facing a problem of confidence, whether they are real or imagined. It is the task of this government to restore and rebuild that confidence."
He pledged that Thailand's stock market, now down at three-year-lows, would be free of political interference.
